title: Momentum and Collisions

cards.b:
A truck is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. A bullet is hard to stop even though it is tiny. Both facts are captured by one idea: momentum.

Momentum explains collisions, rocket flight, airbags and why a cricketer pulls their hands back when catching a fast ball. It is also one of nature's strictest conserved quantities.

Momentum

p = m v

Momentum is a vector with units kg m/s. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has p = 20,000 kg m/s. A 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s has only 4 kg m/s, but it can be stopped by a thin wall because the stopping time is tiny and the force is concentrated.

Newton actually wrote his second law as: force = rate of change of momentum.

cards.h: Impulse: a push over a time
cards.b:
Impulse

F x t = change in momentum

To change momentum you need force acting for some time. The same change can come from a big force for a short time or a small force for a long time.

Catching a fast ball, you move your hands back, lengthening the time. The force drops and your palms are spared. Airbags and crumple zones do the same: they stretch the stopping time so the force on you is smaller.

If no outside force acts on a system, its total momentum stays the same. In a collision, whatever momentum one body loses, the other gains.

This follows from Newton's third law: during a collision the two forces are equal and opposite for the same time, so the momentum changes are equal and opposite.

A rocket works this way too. Gas goes backwards with momentum; the rocket gains equal momentum forwards. No air needed.

Momentum is conserved in every collision (without outside forces). Kinetic energy is not.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy is also conserved. Billiard balls and gas molecules are close to this.
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat, sound and deformation. Most real collisions.
  • Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together, losing the most KE.

A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s hits an identical car at rest and they stick together (see diagram).

Momentum before: 1000 x 20 = 20,000. After: 2000 x v. So v = 10 m/s.

Kinetic energy before: (1/2) x 1000 x 400 = 200,000 J. After: (1/2) x 2000 x 100 = 100,000 J.

Half the energy has gone into crumpling metal and heat. Momentum was conserved; energy was not.

A 0.16 kg ball arrives at 40 m/s and is hit straight back at 40 m/s. Change in momentum = 0.16 x (40 + 40) = 12.8 kg m/s.

If the ball touches the bat for 4 ms (0.004 s), the average force is 12.8 / 0.004 = 3200 N, about the weight of a 330 kg object. Such a short contact time is why the bat feels a sharp sting.

• 'Momentum and kinetic energy are the same thing.' Momentum is mv and has direction; KE is (1/2)mv squared and does not.
  • 'In a crash the bigger vehicle feels the bigger force.' The forces are equal. The lighter vehicle just gets the larger change in velocity.
  • 'Energy is conserved in all collisions.' Total energy is, but mechanical energy usually is not.

Every ISRO launch relies on conservation of momentum: the exhaust of the PSLV pushes it up. Staging, where empty stages drop away, lowers the mass so the same thrust gives a larger acceleration.

On the cricket field, a fielder 'giving' with the ball is the impulse idea. Safety designers of Indian road vehicles use crumple zones and airbags built on the same physics, and India's crash-test programme, Bharat NCAP, began in 2023 to rate vehicles on such safety.

• Momentum p = mv is a vector, in kg m/s.
  • Impulse (force x time) equals change in momentum.
  • Total momentum is conserved when no outside force acts.
  • Elastic collisions also keep kinetic energy; inelastic ones do not.

Think about it

1. Why does a gun recoil backward when it fires a bullet?
2. Why is it better to land on sand than on concrete when you jump?
